title: A King at the Door of the Holy of Holies
sum: After his victory over Antiochus III at Raphia (217 BC), saved from a night attack by an apostate Jew named Dositheus, Ptolemy IV Philopator tours the cities of the region, honoring their shrines. A delegation from Jerusalem welcomes him, and he comes to the temple, sacrifices, and admires it. Then he decides to go into the sanctuary itself. The priests tell him the law: no Gentile, and not all the priests either, may enter; only the high priest, once a year. He insists.

Jerusalem comes apart. Priests lie face down in their robes, girls kept indoors run into the streets, brides leave their wedding rooms, mothers leave their babies. Some young men call for arms, but the elders bring them back to prayer. Even the king's own men join in calling on God. The chapter ends in a roar so loud that the walls seem to cry out.
readings: The opening (1:1-7) follows the battle of Raphia as Polybius tells it, with the king, his sister Arsinoe and Theodotus's raid all in place; C. W. Emmet (1913) found it in substantial agreement with Polybius. The visit to Jerusalem is not reported elsewhere. Victor Tcherikover (1945) called it a legend, while Emmet thought that a real attempt by the king to enter the temple might lie behind the highly colored story.
Read as a story about holy boundaries

The chapter is about a line that no power may cross. A king who has entered every shrine meets one place where his will does not run, and the whole city, from priests to nursing mothers, would rather die than see it crossed.

views.O: The Orthodox Study Bible (2008), which takes its order of books from the Old Testament published with the approval of the Holy Synod of the Church of Greece in 1928, prints 3 Maccabees among the Old Testament books. It also says that the Orthodox Church "has never officially committed itself to a single text and list of Old Testament books." In such a Bible the chapter stands beside the other stories of the temple, such as Heliodorus in 2 Maccabees 3.
views.H: The chapter joins a historical frame (Raphia, 217 BC, as in Polybius 5.79-86) to a temple legend like Heliodorus's in 2 Maccabees 3. Which story depends on which is debated: C. W. Emmet (1913) saw no direct borrowing, only two books of the same school and period. The rule that keeps a Gentile ruler out of the Holy of Holies is the rule of Leviticus 16; the Mishnah, written down later, states it too.
views.J: Jewish tradition tells a similar story of a Greek king and a high priest Simon: the Talmud says Shimon HaTzaddik went out in his priestly robes to meet Alexander the Great, who bowed before him and saved the temple from its enemies (Bavli Yoma 69a). The Mishnah's ranking of holy zones, with Gentiles barred from the inner courts and only the high priest entering the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur, is the rule Ptolemy breaks (Mishnah Kelim 1:8-9), written down about AD 200, later than this book.
views.N: The same rules stand behind the New Testament: Hebrews 9:7 says the high priest alone enters, once a year, and Paul was mobbed because people thought "he has brought Greeks into the temple and made this holy place common" (Acts 21:28). The first Christians knew how fiercely Jews defended the sanctuary's boundaries.
views.W: Catholic and Protestant churches do not count the book as Scripture. They read the chapter as a witness to Jewish devotion to the temple in the Greek period, set beside 2 Chronicles 26 and 2 Maccabees 3, which tell of rulers struck at the holy place.

deep.b: Polybius tells the campaign of 217 BC in detail (Histories 5.79-86): Ptolemy IV and Arsinoe led the army; Theodotus, a former officer of Ptolemy, raided the camp by night but searched the wrong tent and killed the king's physician (5.81); the king spoke to his troops and Arsinoe addressed the phalanx (5.83); Ptolemy won, and the towns of Coele-Syria honored him with crowns and sacrifices (5.86). 3 Maccabees keeps this frame but adds what Polybius lacks: a Jew, Dositheus, who saved the king, and Arsinoe's loosened hair and promise of gold. The writer is not writing history for its own sake; he uses a well-known victory to set the stage for a king at the height of his pride.

deep.title: Two tents (Claude's theory)
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The chapter opens with a man who tries to enter a king's tent at night to kill him and is stopped by a Jew's quick thinking (1:2-3). It then shows a king who tries to enter God's house and is stopped by God (1:10-2:22). The sanctuary began as a tent: God says, "I have walked about in a tent, in a tabernacle" (2 Samuel 7:6). The writer may mean the pairing: Ptolemy owes his life to the fact that his tent was guarded, yet he will not respect the guarded dwelling of God. I have not seen this pairing argued in published work.

echoes: 2 Maccabees 3:13-40; Leviticus 16:2; Hebrews 9:7; 2 Chronicles 26:16-20; Daniel 11:10-12; Acts 21:28

settings.what: The priests' answer and the king's demand
settings.to: Ptolemy IV, in the temple courts
settings.when: after his sacrifice, when he decides to enter the sanctuary
settings.why: The priests read him the law to stop him without force: no Gentile, and only the high priest once a year. The king's answers show a ruler who treats every shrine as his to enter.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt, above all Alexandria, for whom the temple far away in Jerusalem was a sign of their identity. The date is debated.
views: C. W. Emmet (1913) dates the book to about 100 BC. Its official language, the greeting of its letters and its spellings match Egyptian papyri of that time, and the census word of 2:28 (laographia) has been found in Ptolemaic papyri. He reports that Wendland and Thackeray put it at 100-80 BC.

Victor Tcherikover (1945) argued that the census of 2:28, which the book treats as a mark of slavery, is the census under Augustus that listed those who paid the poll tax, so the book was written then. Emmet reports that Wilcken had earlier taken laographia as a Roman-period word for the same reason.

Heinrich Ewald linked the book with the emperor Caligula's attempt to set up his image in the temple and with the attacks on Alexandria's Jews in his reign. Emmet, who reports the view, answers that the book lacks the marks of that story.

settings.by: The priests, the people of Jerusalem, and even the king's own officers
settings.to: God, "the one who holds every power"
settings.when: as the king presses toward the sanctuary
settings.why: The prayer is the only weapon the book approves: the young men who call for arms are brought back to it (1:23). It prepares for Simon's prayer and God's answer in chapter 2.
settings.readers: Jews of Egypt who had no army of their own and lived under a foreign king; the scene teaches them to trust prayer.

settings.what: The elders' plea to the king
settings.by: The senior men at the king's side
settings.when: as he presses on toward the sanctuary
settings.why: To talk the king out of his plan by persuasion, after the law read to him has failed. He brushes them aside, so the only help left is prayer (1:27).
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt; even the king's own advisers are shown knowing he is wrong. On the date, see 1:11-15.

title: Simon's Prayer and the Brand of Dionysus
sum: The high priest Simon kneels before the sanctuary and prays. He calls on the King of the heavens, recalls how God destroyed the giants with the Flood, burned Sodom, drowned Pharaoh, chose Jerusalem and promised to hear prayer made there. He confesses Israel's sins and begs God not to let the lawless boast that they have trampled his house. God hears. He shakes the king like a reed until he lies paralyzed and speechless, and his men drag him out.

The king recovers but feels no regret. Back in Alexandria he sets up a stone pillar: Jews who will not sacrifice are to be registered in the census, reduced to the status of slaves, and branded with the ivy leaf of Dionysus; those who join the mysteries may become equal citizens. A few give in. Most refuse, try to buy their way out, and shun those who went over.
readings: Simon's prayer works like the prayers of Solomon (1 Kings 8) and Hezekiah: it rehearses God's past rescues, confesses sin, and asks God to act for his own name. The blow that follows is the answer.

For the writer the danger in Alexandria is not only death but a bargain: citizenship and status for those who give up the law. Chapter 2 sets that choice before the reader before the persecution begins.

views.O: The Orthodox Study Bible prints 3 Maccabees in its Old Testament, along with a Daniel that includes the Hymn of the Three Young Men. In such a Bible Simon's prayer can be read beside that hymn and the other prayers of the Greek Old Testament: a priest pleading for his people in words drawn from Scripture.
views.H: Historians use the details of this chapter to date the book. C. W. Emmet (1913) points out that Dionysus was the family god of the Ptolemies and that the census word laographia is found in Ptolemaic papyri; Victor Tcherikover (1945) read the census as the one taken under Augustus. Tcherikover also thought that 2:28-29, without the mention of Jews, came from a historical source of Philopator's reign.
views.J: The prayer draws on the Septuagint: the giants of Genesis 6:4, Solomon's "heaven of heaven" (1 Kings 8:27) and Psalm 79:8. C. W. Emmet (1913) takes the high priest Simon to be the one Sirach praises (Sirach 50:1-21), and the Talmud's Simon the Righteous (Bavli Yoma 69a) is remembered for saving the temple before a Greek king.
views.N: Christian commentators on Revelation 13:16, such as the Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges and the commentary of Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, cite this brand beside the mark of the beast. The comparison is made by later readers; no early Christian writer is cited for it here. A ruler struck by God for pride appears in Acts 12:23.
views.W: Western readers who do not count the book as Scripture read Simon's prayer as Jewish piety of the Second Temple period, and compare its story of God striking a proud king with those that are in their Bibles (2 Chronicles 26; Daniel 4; Acts 12).

deep.b: The prayer (2:2-20) has three parts. First, praise: God the Creator and just Sovereign who judges the proud (2:2-3). Second, history: the giants and the Flood, Sodom, Pharaoh and the sea (2:4-8), then the choice of Jerusalem and the promise to hear prayer there (2:9-12). Third, plea: Israel's sins, the profane man's threat, and the request for mercy "at this very hour" (2:13-20). Each example is a proud power destroyed, and the idea of arrogance runs through it, in several Greek words (2:3, 5, 17, 21). The priest Eleazar's prayer in 6:2-15 follows the same plan, with Pharaoh, Sennacherib, the furnace, the lions' den and Jonah.

The pillar's decree (2:28-30) has three parts: Jews who will not sacrifice lose access to "their temples"; all Jews are put on the census rolls and lowered to the status of slaves, with the ivy leaf branded on them; and any who join the Dionysiac mysteries become equal citizens with the Alexandrians. C. W. Emmet (1913) notes that Dionysus was the family god of the Ptolemies, and that the census word laographia meant, in Ptolemaic papyri, a tax list of people who were mostly native Egyptians. Victor Tcherikover (1945) read the book as treating the pursuit of civic rights in Alexandria as a betrayal, and the census as the one under Augustus. The book thus turns a real hope of Alexandrian Jews, civic equality, into a temptation.

echoes: Genesis 6:4; Genesis 19:24; Exodus 14:28; 1 Kings 8:27-30; 2 Chronicles 20:9; Psalm 79:8; Ezekiel 16:49; Revelation 13:16; 2 Maccabees 3:24-34; 2 Maccabees 6:7

settings.to: God, before the sanctuary, in the hearing of priests and people
settings.when: as Ptolemy is about to enter the sanctuary
settings.why: To move God to act by recalling his past judgments on the proud and his promise to hear prayer in this place, while confessing Israel's sins. In the story it is the turning point: God answers at once.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt, who prayed toward Jerusalem from far away; the prayer gives them words for their own crises, as Eleazar's prayer will in 6:2-15. On the date, see the setting of 1:11-15.

settings.to: The Jews of Alexandria, in a public inscription in the palace quarter
settings.why: The decree binds every Jew in the city: sacrifice or lose access to worship, be listed in the census and lowered to slave status, and be branded for Dionysus. Its escape clause, citizenship for those initiated into the mysteries, is meant to split the community.
settings.readers: Alexandrian Jews who cared about their civic standing; the story warns that status bought with apostasy is betrayal.

title: The Slander and the King's Letter
sum: Enraged that most Jews refuse his offer, the king orders all the Jews of the countryside gathered and killed. Hostile neighbors spread rumors: the Jews keep apart in worship and food, and so they cannot be loyal. The writer answers that the Jews were loyal to the kings and respected by all, and that the Greeks of the city pitied them and some neighbors secretly promised help.

Then comes the king's letter to his governors. It retells his visit to Jerusalem as an act of kindness that the Jews met with arrogance, claims that he offered them citizenship, and calls them traitors and barbarians. All Jews, with wives and children, are to be sent to him in chains to die. Anyone who hides a Jew will be tortured to death with his household; informers will be rewarded; any place that shelters a Jew will be burned.
readings: The chapter follows the pattern of Esther 3 and the Greek Esther's Addition B: a slander that one people keeps its own laws, a royal letter ordering death for all, and the sense of a whole people at a king's mercy. The reversal will come, as in Esther, with a second letter (7:1-9).
Read as an answer to slander

The writer lets the charges be heard, then answers them: the Jews do keep apart in food and worship, but they are loyal and just. The chapter is a defense of the Jewish community to its own members, and perhaps to friendly outsiders.

views.O: In Orthodox Bibles, such as the Orthodox Study Bible, this chapter stands in the same Old Testament as Esther and Daniel, whose stories of false accusation and rescue it follows.
views.H: The letter is the writer's composition, written in the style of a royal Greek letter. C. W. Emmet (1913) found its official language, such as the greeting "greetings and good health," matched in Egyptian papyri and in the letters of the Letter of Aristeas. Its charges against the Jews (separateness in food and worship, disloyalty) are the ones the Letter of Aristeas answers (Aristeas 128 and following), and the question of citizenship in Alexandria is one of the details scholars use to date the book.
views.J: The chapter is part of a family of stories in which a foreign king decrees the death of the Jews and is reversed, with Esther at its head. The book says the days of rescue were fixed as a yearly festival and kept (6:36; 7:19), as Purim is in Esther; nothing outside the book shows that this festival was kept. C. W. Emmet (1913) notes that Josephus tells of a day the Jews of Alexandria kept for a different rescue from elephants under a later king, Ptolemy VIII (see the note on 7:19).
views.N: Early Christians faced the same charges: that they would not join the gods' rites and were enemies of the state (Acts 16:20-21; 17:7). The threat against those who shelter Jews, and the reward for informers, recall the Gospels' warning that family members will hand one another over (Mark 13:12).
views.W: Catholic and Protestant readers, who do not count the book as Scripture, read the chapter as a witness to the slanders Jews faced in the Greek world and to the faith that answered them.

deep.b: The letter of 3:12-29 has the parts of a royal Greek letter: greeting (3:12), wish for health (3:13), the background (3:14-24), the order (3:25-26), penalties and rewards (3:27-29). Its claims answer the narrator point by point: the narrator says the king was struck down in the temple (2:21-22); the letter says he spared the Jews out of kindness (3:18). The narrator says the citizenship offer required initiation (2:30); the letter calls it a gift the Jews spurned (3:21-23). In 7:1-9 the same king will write a second letter that takes it all back, as the Persian king does in the Greek Esther (Addition E).

echoes: Esther 3:8-15; Esther 8:9-13; Daniel 1:8; Daniel 3:29; Ezra 6:11; Leviticus 11; Hebrews 11:35

settings.by: Men "who had joined together to do the race harm"
settings.to: The people of Alexandria and the king's circle
settings.when: while the king's order against the Jews of the countryside is being arranged
settings.why: To make the Jews look disloyal by pointing to their separateness in worship and food. The narrator records it so as to refute it (3:3-5, 8-10).
settings.readers: Jews of Egypt who heard such charges from their neighbors; the book gives them an answer and reminds them that many Greeks were friendly.

settings.to: The governors and soldiers in Egypt and every district
settings.when: after the Jews refuse the offer of citizenship by initiation
settings.why: An order with the force of law: every Jew, with wife and children, is to be sent in chains to die; whoever hides a Jew dies with his household; informers get the victim's property, two thousand drachmas and freedom; any place that hides a Jew is to be burned. It binds officials and every subject in the kingdom.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt; the letter, like Esther's, lets them feel the threat in full before God reverses it in chapters 5-7. On the date, see the setting of 1:11-15.
